title: What is performance testing — testing how your system behaves under load — and what are the types: Load Testing (normal expected load), Stress Testing (beyond normal, find breaking point), Spike Testing (sudden burst of traffic), Endurance/Soak Testing (sustained load over long time to find memory leaks)?
shortTitle: What is performance testing and its types

s1_definition.profdef: Performance testing evaluates how a system behaves under load rather than whether it is functionally correct, measuring attributes such as response time, throughput, and error rate as concurrent demand varies. Its main types are load testing, which applies the normal expected load to confirm the system meets its targets; stress testing, which pushes beyond normal load to find the breaking point and observe failure behavior; spike testing, which applies a sudden sharp burst of traffic to check the system copes with abrupt surges; and endurance or soak testing, which applies sustained load over a long period to reveal problems like memory leaks and resource exhaustion that only appear over time.
s1_definition.analogy: Functional testing asks whether the National Bank of India transfer works; performance testing asks whether it still works when thousands of customers transfer at once. Load testing is a normal busy day, confirming the bank handles its usual rush smoothly. Stress testing keeps piling on more and more customers until the bank buckles, to learn where the limit is and whether it fails gracefully. Spike testing is a sudden flood, like everyone logging in the instant salaries are credited, to see if the bank survives the shock. And soak testing keeps a steady stream of customers flowing for many hours or days, to catch slow problems like a leak that only shows up after long running, the way a small drip eventually floods a room.
s1_definition.oneliner: Performance testing measures how a system behaves under load, using load testing for normal demand, stress testing to find the breaking point, spike testing for sudden bursts, and endurance or soak testing for sustained load that reveals leaks over time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Performance testing evaluates how a system behaves under load rather than whether it is functionally correct, measuring attributes such as response time, throughput, and error rate as concurrent demand varies. Its main types are load testing, which applies the normal expected load to confirm the system meets its targets; stress testing, which pushes beyond normal load to find the breaking point and observe failure behavior; spike testing, which applies a sudden sharp burst of traffic to check the system copes with abrupt surges; and endurance or soak testing, which applies sustained load over a long period to reveal problems like memory leaks and resource exhaustion that only appear over time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Functional testing asks whether the National Bank of India transfer works; performance testing asks whether it still works when thousands of customers transfer at once. Load testing is a normal busy day, confirming the bank handles its usual rush smoothly. Stress testing keeps piling on more and more customers until the bank buckles, to learn where the limit is and whether it fails gracefully. Spike testing is a sudden flood, like everyone logging in the instant salaries are credited, to see if the bank survives the shock. And soak testing keeps a steady stream of customers flowing for many hours or days, to catch slow problems like a leak that only shows up after long running, the way a small drip eventually floods a room.

**One line to remember:** Performance testing measures how a system behaves under load, using load testing for normal demand, stress testing to find the breaking point, spike testing for sudden bursts, and endurance or soak testing for sustained load that reveals leaks over time.

sections.s2_technical:
Performance testing is a non-functional discipline that answers how well the system performs under concurrency, not whether a feature returns the correct value. The core measurements are response time, how long a request takes, often reported as percentiles; throughput, how many requests per second the system handles; and error rate, the fraction of requests that fail, which tends to rise as the system is pushed. You design performance tests around realistic scenarios and a defined workload model, number of concurrent users, request mix, and ramp pattern, and you run them against an environment that resembles production closely enough for the results to be meaningful.

Load testing applies the normal and peak expected load the system is designed for and verifies it meets its performance targets, the service-level objectives, at that load, for example that the ninety-fifth-percentile response time stays under two hundred milliseconds at the expected transactions per second with an acceptable error rate. It validates that the system is adequately provisioned for real demand and is the baseline performance test. Stress testing deliberately pushes past the normal load, increasing concurrency or request rate until the system degrades or fails, to find the breaking point, the capacity ceiling, and to observe how it fails, whether it degrades gracefully with rising latency and controlled errors or collapses catastrophically, and whether it recovers when the load eases. Stress testing informs capacity planning and resilience, and reveals the first resource to saturate, CPU, memory, connection pools, or a downstream dependency.

Spike testing applies a sudden, sharp increase in traffic over a very short time, rather than a gradual ramp, to check how the system handles abrupt surges such as a flash event or, in banking, the instant salaries are credited or a festival sale begins. It tests autoscaling reaction time, queueing, and whether the sudden burst causes timeouts, dropped requests, or cascading failures. Endurance or soak testing applies a sustained, moderate load for a long duration, hours or days, to surface problems that only manifest over time: memory leaks that slowly exhaust the heap, connection or file-handle leaks, log or disk growth, cache bloat, or gradual performance degradation. These are invisible in short tests but cause production incidents after the system has been running a while, so soak testing is how you catch them before customers do.

The senior nuances are to define clear objectives and a realistic workload model before testing, because a test without targets and a representative mix produces meaningless numbers; to run against a production-like environment and data volume, since performance is sensitive to configuration and data size; to report percentiles rather than averages because averages hide the slow tail that users feel; to monitor the system under test, not just the client, so you can see which resource saturates; and to treat these types as answering different questions, is it fast enough at expected load, where does it break, does it survive a surge, and does it stay healthy over time, so a mature performance strategy uses all four rather than one. In a bank these matter acutely because peak events like salary day and month-end settlement are predictable surges, and a slow or failing system during them directly affects customers and compliance, so load, stress, spike, and soak testing together give the confidence that the system will hold under real conditions.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must confirm the transfer API meets its latency and error targets at the expected peak, which is exactly load testing.

Problem 2 — It must find where the system breaks and whether it fails gracefully, which is stress testing, and it must survive the salary-day surge, which is spike testing.

Problem 3 — It must confirm the system does not slowly leak memory over a long run, which is endurance or soak testing.

In the mini-project we build a simple performance simulator: a model of a service with a capacity, and four test routines, load, stress, spike, and soak, that report response time, throughput, and error rate, plus a soak routine that detects a simulated memory leak, so each type is concrete. We write a Java harness.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a service model that sustains one thousand transactions per second, with latency and error rate that worsen past capacity and a memory leak toggle for soak.

Step 1: The load test applies nine hundred transactions per second, within capacity, and reports a low ninety-fifth-percentile latency and near-zero errors, meeting the service-level objective, confirming the system handles normal peak demand.

Step 2: The stress test pushes to twelve hundred, sixteen hundred, and two thousand transactions per second, past capacity, and reports latency rising sharply and error rate climbing, revealing the breaking point and that the system degrades under overload rather than silently.

Step 3: The spike test jumps instantly from one hundred to eighteen hundred transactions per second, and the before-and-after shows latency and errors surging, which tests whether autoscaling or queueing lets the system survive an abrupt burst like salary day.

Step 4: The soak test runs eight hundred transactions per second for a simulated twelve hours with the leak enabled, accumulating leaked memory each hour.

Step 5: After twelve hours the accumulated leak exceeds the threshold, so the soak test flags a memory leak that would eventually crash the service in production, demonstrating exactly the class of slow problem that only sustained testing reveals.

Final output:

```

2026-10-30 10:24:40 [INFO] STRESS @1600TPS: p95=680ms err=60.0% (breaking/degrading)
2026-10-30 10:24:40 [INFO] STRESS @2000TPS: p95=1000ms err=60.0% (breaking/degrading)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Performance testing evaluates how a system behaves under load rather than whether a feature is functionally correct, measuring response time, usually as percentiles, throughput in requests per second, and error rate as demand varies. I always start from a defined workload model, the concurrent users, the request mix, and the ramp pattern, and clear service-level targets, run against a production-like environment, because without those the numbers are meaningless.

There are four main types, each answering a different question. Load testing applies the normal and peak expected load and verifies the system meets its targets, for example the ninety-fifth-percentile latency staying under two hundred milliseconds at the expected transactions per second with an acceptable error rate; it is the baseline that confirms adequate provisioning for real demand. Stress testing deliberately pushes past normal load until the system degrades or fails, to find the breaking point and, just as importantly, to observe how it fails, whether it degrades gracefully with rising latency and controlled errors or collapses, and whether it recovers when load eases, which informs capacity planning and resilience. Spike testing applies a sudden sharp burst rather than a gradual ramp, to see whether the system survives an abrupt surge like the instant salaries are credited, testing autoscaling reaction, queueing, and whether the burst causes timeouts or cascading failures. And endurance or soak testing applies a sustained moderate load for hours or days to surface problems that only appear over time, memory leaks, connection leaks, disk growth, and gradual degradation, which are invisible in short tests but cause production incidents after the system has been running a while.

The senior points I add are to report percentiles not averages, because averages hide the slow tail users feel, to monitor the system under test so I can see which resource saturates first, and to treat the four types as complementary questions, fast enough at expected load, where does it break, does it survive a surge, and does it stay healthy over time, so a mature strategy uses all four. At the National Bank of India these mattered acutely because salary day and month-end settlement are predictable surges, so I load-tested against the expected peak, stress-tested to find our ceiling and confirm graceful degradation, spike-tested the salary-credit burst, and ran a twelve-hour soak that once caught a slow memory leak that would have crashed the transfer service in production. Being able to define performance testing and crisply distinguish load, stress, spike, and soak by the question each answers is what shows an interviewer I understand performance as a first-class quality concern for a bank, not an afterthought.
